claims.claim: The prose is shoddy and inconsistent while also being heavily repetitive.
claims.source: Jarosława Radowski (@sophistry), 'Why GRRM's A Song of Ice and Fire is Bad Literature', Medium, 6 Mar 2021 (full text read from the Medium RSS feed)
claims.quote: His prose is shoddy and inconsistent

claims.claim: Readers themselves mock recurring formulas such as 'as useless as nipples on a breastplate'.
claims.source: Jarosława Radowski (@sophistry), 'Why GRRM's A Song of Ice and Fire is Bad Literature', Medium, 6 Mar 2021 (full text read from the Medium RSS feed)
claims.quote: as useless as nipples on a breastplate

claims.claim: Dialogue is grandiose and swear-ridden but has little substance; the Darkstar 'I am of the night' exchange is cringeworthy and its symbolism incomprehensible.
claims.source: Jarosława Radowski (@sophistry), 'Why GRRM's A Song of Ice and Fire is Bad Literature', Medium, 6 Mar 2021 (full text read from the Medium RSS feed)
claims.quote: behind the ostentatious fluff, there’s little substance

claims.claim: Martin is obsessed with expendable details (every feast dish, a character's gynecomastia), which bloats the books.
claims.source: Jarosława Radowski (@sophistry), 'Why GRRM's A Song of Ice and Fire is Bad Literature', Medium, 6 Mar 2021 (full text read from the Medium RSS feed)

claims.claim: The Oberyn–Mountain duel has no symbolism, metaphor or manipulated time and no build-up to catharsis, only the shock of a hero dying; the stableboy's death is sensational violence.
claims.source: Jarosława Radowski (@sophistry), 'Why GRRM's A Song of Ice and Fire is Bad Literature', Medium, 6 Mar 2021 (full text read from the Medium RSS feed)
claims.quote: No literary devices such as symbolism, metaphors, even the fucking pacing

claims.claim: The duel's repeated 'You raped her. You murdered her. You killed her children' refrain is reproduced at length as evidence of flat, unbuilt violence.
claims.source: Jarosława Radowski (@sophistry), 'Why GRRM's A Song of Ice and Fire is Bad Literature', Medium, 6 Mar 2021 (full text read from the Medium RSS feed)

claims.claim: The summary verdict is that the prose is not poetic, the dialogue can be childish and the story convoluted.
claims.source: Jarosława Radowski (@sophistry), 'Why GRRM's A Song of Ice and Fire is Bad Literature', Medium, 6 Mar 2021 (full text read from the Medium RSS feed)
claims.quote: His prose is not poetic, his dialogue can be childish

claims.claim: Because viewpoint characters must lack foresight of their fate, POV status itself predicts tribulation and makes the 'anyone can die' twists predictable.
claims.source: Jarosława Radowski (@sophistry), 'Why GRRM's A Song of Ice and Fire is Bad Literature', Medium, 6 Mar 2021 (full text read from the Medium RSS feed)
claims.quote: readers already expect their POV characters to experience tribulation

claims.claim: Jaime's 'arc' is perception development: Martin warps the reader's view via backstory rather than changing the character.
claims.source: Jarosława Radowski (@sophistry), 'Why GRRM's A Song of Ice and Fire is Bad Literature', Medium, 6 Mar 2021 (full text read from the Medium RSS feed)
claims.quote: What passes off as “character development” is actually “perception development.”

claims.claim: Characters are one-dimensional, focused on singular interests, and sortable into a 'Hall of Tropes' (Patriarch, Ideal Hero, Ax-Crazy).
claims.source: Jarosława Radowski (@sophistry), 'Why GRRM's A Song of Ice and Fire is Bad Literature', Medium, 6 Mar 2021 (full text read from the Medium RSS feed)
claims.quote: one-dimensional and comically focused on singular interests

claims.claim: Cersei may be the only viewpoint character who is completely unsympathetic; her POV chapters repeatedly tell rather than show that she would fare better as a man.
claims.source: Ryan B. (guest), 'What's Really Wrong with A Song of Ice and Fire', Ordinary Times, 31 Aug 2011
claims.quote: We are told repeatedly in her POV chapters

claims.claim: Dany reads as a white saviour whose errors cost her little, and Drogo as a Noble Savage; the essay is about characterization and politics, not sentence craft.
claims.source: Ryan B. (guest), 'What's Really Wrong with A Song of Ice and Fire', Ordinary Times, 31 Aug 2011

claims.claim: The books are great and hold a mirror to our world but suffer from the faults they try to expose.
claims.source: Ryan B. (guest), 'What's Really Wrong with A Song of Ice and Fire', Ordinary Times, 31 Aug 2011

claims.claim: For a thousand pages almost nothing happens and then there are cliffhangers; the book is too long and painfully slow.
claims.source: Erik Kain, 'Review: A Dance with Dragons', Ordinary Times, 8 Aug 2011
claims.quote: It’s too long. It’s painfully slow.

claims.claim: The book feels unedited; a bold editor with a red pen could have cut it by nearly half.
claims.source: Erik Kain, 'Review: A Dance with Dragons', Ordinary Times, 8 Aug 2011
claims.quote: A good edit would have slashed this book by nearly half

verdicts.note: Medium live URL 403; reached via Wayback raw capture 20250221030333id_. Page (Writing Style): "His prose is shoddy and inconsistent, yet it still gets heavily repetitive." Quote verbatim; both limbs (shoddy/inconsistent, heavily repetitive) on the page.

Page: "His own readers poke fun at this, pointing out common phrases such as “[X is] as useless as nipples on a breastplate.”" Quote verbatim; 'readers themselves mock' = 'his own readers poke fun', 'recurring formulas' = 'common phrases'.

Page: "GRRM does put an effort into the dialogue, drafting grandiose statements and swear-ridden rants. Yet behind the ostentatious fluff, there’s little substance in them." Darkstar limb: “No. Men call me Darkstar, and I am of the night.” then "it’s incredibly cringeworthy" and "the symbolism is not comprehendible." All four limbs on page.

Page (Details): "GRRM is completely obsessed with expendable details. Is this really the epitome of worldbuilding, wasting ink over obesity-onset gynecomastia and every dish laid out on a feast?" Bloat limb: "if he cut down on this superfluous bullshit, the books would be a lot thinner and straightforward."

Page: "No literary devices such as symbolism, metaphors, even the fucking pacing. While there is a climax, the scene does not build itself up to it: there is no intensity in the air, and time is not manipulated. Catharsis is missing, and the only feelings a reader has for Oberyn’s death is shock due to the element of hero invincibility." Stableboy limb: "It’s a great example of sensational violence." Every limb supported.

Claim carries no quote field, but its embedded refrain “You raped her. You murdered her. You killed her children.” appears verbatim and is reproduced seven times in the block-quoted duel excerpt; the passage is immediately followed by "No literary devices such as symbolism, metaphors, even the fucking pacing... the scene does not build itself up to it," i.e. used as evidence of flat, unbuilt violence.
Page (Conclusion): "His prose is not poetic, his dialogue can be childish, and his story is convoluted." Quote verbatim; all three limbs are the article's own summary verdict.

Page: "Since every POV character GRRM creates must lack the foresight of their fate, readers are already aware of their impending doom." and "Being aware of this irony completely ruins every plot twist, since readers already expect their POV characters to experience tribulation." The 'anyone can die' limb: the article names GRRM’s “Any[one] Can Die” plot twists under heading 2, "By overusing unpredictable plot arcs, GRRM sets himself up to become more predictable."

Page: "What passes off as “character development” is actually “perception development.” Instead of putting effort into developing his characters, GRRM decides to warp the reader’s perceptions instead. To make Jaime a sympathetic character, GRRM develops Jaime’s backstory..." Quote verbatim including both curly-quoted terms.

Page: "GRRM’s characters tend to be one-dimensional and comically focused on singular interests"; "GRRM has a “Hall of Tropes” filled with predictable characters"; and the exercise lists Tropes: "- The Patriarch - Ideal Hero - Ax-Crazy". All three named tropes present verbatim.

ordinary-times.com fetched live (HTTP 200, browser UA). Byline confirms Guest Authors, "~ by Ryan B.", August 31, 2011. Page: "She is quite possibly the only viewpoint character who is completely unsympathetic." and "We are told repeatedly in her POV chapters that she wouldn’t have as much trouble if she were a man, but it’s never clear how much trouble she has as a woman." The tell-not-show limb is the article's own contrast.

Page: "a feminist icon she ain’t" verbatim; "She is sort of a white savior, as noted above"; "she never suffers much for it" (errors cost her little); "Drogo is a pretty quintessential Noble Savage." Final limb checked by absence: the article body contains zero occurrences of 'prose' or 'style' and no sentence-craft discussion — it argues characterization, race and gender politics.

Closing paragraph verbatim: "These books are great. They hold up a mirror to our own world and invite discussion of its faults. But they aren’t perfect. They also suffer from the faults they are often trying to expose." Every limb present.
